{{Use British English|date=June 2025}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=June 2025}}

'''Peter John Twin''' (born 26 July 1939 in London)<ref>biographical information from ''American Men and Women of Science'', Thomson Gale 2004</ref> is a British experimental nuclear physicist. He is known for his research into the structure  of atomic nuclei, based upon his pioneering work on techniques of [[Gamma spectroscopy|gamma ray spectroscopy]] and, specifically, the Total Energy Suppression Shield Array (TESSA).<ref name=CV/><ref>The original TESSA used 6 germanium detectors with NaI crystals in the suppression shields. Both TESSA2 and TESSA3 replaced the NaI crystals with bismuth germanate. TESSA 2 had 6 germanium detectors, but TESSA 3 was upgraded to 16 germanium detectors.</ref>

==Education and career==
Peter J. Twin graduated from the [[University of Liverpool]] with a BSc in 1960 and a PhD in 1964. At the University of Liverpool, he became a lecturer in 1964, a Senior Lecturer in 1973, a Reader in 1979,<ref name=CV>{{cite web|title=Resume of Professor Peter Twin's Career (Meitner Prize archive)|website=Physics Department, University of Glasgow, EPS/NPB (physics.gla.ac.uk/~ianm/epsnpb/organization)|year=2004|url=http://www.physics.gla.ac.uk/~ianm/epsnpb/organization/activities/meitner/2004/resume_PT.ps}}</ref> Sir James Chadwick Professor of [[Experimental physics|Experimental Physics]] in 1987, Lyon James Professor of Physics in 1997,<ref name=WetherillAward>{{cite web|title=Peter John Twin, Wetherill Award|website=The Franklin Institute Awards|date=15 January 2014 |url=https://www.fi.edu/laureates/peter-john-twin}}</ref> and a Senior Fellow and Professor Emeritus in 2001. From 1983 to 1987 he was also Head of the Nuclear Structure Facility at the [[Daresbury Laboratory]], which is about 30 kilometres from Liverpool. For the academic year 1968–1969 he was a visiting professor at the [[University of Alberta]].<ref name=CV/>

In 1986, his science team discovered [[Superdeformation|superdeformed nuclei]] with a high [[nuclear spin|spin]] (with an observation of a [[yrast]] line in the [[Gamma spectroscopy|gamma spectrum]]).<ref>{{cite journal|author=Twin, P.J.|author2=Nyakó, B.M.|author3=Nelson, A.H.|author4=Simpson, J.|author5=Bentley, M.A.|author6=Cranmer-Gordon, H.W.|author7=Forsyth, P.D.|author8=Howe, D.|author9=Mokhtar, A.R.|author10=Morrison, J.D.|author11=Sharpey-Schafer, J.F.|year=1986|title=Observation of a Discrete-Line Superdeformed Band up to 60 ℏ in <sup>152</sup>Dy |journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=57|issue=7|pages=811–814|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.57.811|pmid=10034167 |bibcode=1986PhRvL..57..811T }} (over 900 citations)</ref> In 1991 [[Daniel Kleppner]] judged Twin's discovery of superdeformed nuclei to be one most important discoveries in physics in the years from 1986 to 1991.<ref>{{citation|author=Kleppner, Daniel|periodical=Physics Today|title=A Lesson in Humility|volume=44|issue=12|at=p.&nbsp;9|date=December 1991|language=German|doi =10.1063/1.2810343
| bibcode=1991PhT....44l...9K }} Kleppner's article criticizes the National Research Council's 1986 preview of physics (Brinkman Report, chaired by [[William F. Brinkman]]). {{cite journal|date=27 December 1991|author=Schewe, Phillip F.|author2=Stein, Ben|title=Physics News Update|issue=# 60|journal=American Institute of Physics Bulletin|url=https://www.aip.org/pnu/1991/physnews.060.htm |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040906071850/https://www.aip.org/pnu/1991/physnews.060.htm |archive-date=2004-09-06 }}</ref> In retrospect, the phenomenon was also observed in 1962 when [[spontaneous fission]] of [[isomer]]s in heavy nuclei was discovered by Sergey Polikanov (1926–1994).

In 1991, Twin received the [[John Price Wetherill Medal]] from the [[Franklin Institute]].<ref name=WetherillAward/> In 1991 he also won the [[American Physical Society]]'s [[Tom W. Bonner Prize in Nuclear Physics]].<ref>{{cite web|title=1991 Tom W. Bonner Prize in Nuclear Physics Recipient, Peter J. Twin|website=American Physical Society|url=https://www.aps.org/programs/honors/prizes/prizerecipient.cfm?last_nm=Twin&first_nm=Peter&year=1991}}</ref>

Following the success of TESSA III, he collaborated with Francis Beck, director of the ''Centre de recherches nucléaires'' (CRN) at [[Strasbourg]], on leading the French-British development of the more advanced gamma ray detectors of the Eurogam project. Eurogam I became operational in 1992 at Daresbury, and Eurogam II became operational in 1994 at Strasbourg.<ref name=CV/><ref>{{cite journal|author=Balter, Michael|author-link=Michael Balter|title=Powerful new detectors spy on strange spinning nuclei|journal=Science|volume=266|issue=5184|year=1994|page=362|doi=10.1126/science.266.5184.362|pmid=17816672 |bibcode=1994Sci...266..362B }}</ref> The detector arrays of Eurogam culminated in the EUROBALL detector array (which became operational in 1996).<ref name=CV/><ref>{{cite journal|title=The EUROBALL gamma ray detector|author=de Angelis, G.|author2=Bracco, A.|author2-link=Angela Bracco|author3=Curien, D.|journal=Europhysics News|year=2003|volume=34|issue=5|url=http://www0.mi.infn.it/~wieland/paper_wieland/articleeuroball.html}}</ref>

Twin was made [[OBE]] in 1991<ref name=CV/> and elected in 1993 a Fellow of the [[Royal Society]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Peter Twin, Biography|website=Royal Society|url=https://royalsociety.org/people/peter-twin-12447/}}</ref> In 2004 he was awarded, jointly with Bent Herskind, the [[European Physical Society]]'s [[Lise Meitner Prize]].<ref>{{cite web|title=Recipients of the 2004 Lise Meitner Prize for Nuclear Science Awarded by the European Physical Society (Meitner Prize archive)|website=Physics Department, University of Glasgow, EPS/NPB (physics.gla.ac.uk/~ianm/epsnpb/organization)|url=http://www.physics.gla.ac.uk/~ianm/epsnpb/organization/activities/meitner/2004/meitner_2004.html}}</ref>
